(b) $R = 20 / 32 = 0.625$ [0.5]
(c) missed $32 - 20 = 12$ (FN) · false alarms $25 - 20 = 5$ (FP) [0.5]
Answer: (a) 0.8 · (b) 0.625 · (c) 12 missed, 5 false alarms
124⭐⭐Raise the threshold2 pts · ~4 min
An image has 5 people. The detector's boxes, sorted by score, were matched to them:
score0.90.80.70.60.40.3
matchTPTPFPTPFPTP
Compute precision and recall at thresholds (a) 0.75, (b) 0.5, (c) 0.25. (d) Describe the trade.
Show solution
(a) 2 boxes, both TP: $P = 1.0$, $R = 2/5 = 0.4$ [0.5]
(b) 4 boxes, 3 TP: $P = 0.75$, $R = 0.6$ [0.5]
(c) 6 boxes, 4 TP: $P \approx 0.67$, $R = 0.8$ [0.5]
(d) a lower threshold finds more people (recall up) but lets in more false alarms (precision down) [0.5]
Answer: (a) 1.0 / 0.4 · (b) 0.75 / 0.6 · (c) 0.67 / 0.8

B · One-stage detection

Slides for this part →
125⭐Count the cells1.5 pts · ~3 min
A YOLO detector gets a $416 \times 416$ image and predicts on grids with strides 8, 16 and 32. (a) How many cells does each grid have? (b) How many predictions in all?
Show solution
(a) $416/8 = 52$ → $52^2 = 2704$ · $416/16 = 26$ → $676$ · $416/32 = 13$ → $169$ [1]
(b) $2704 + 676 + 169 = 3549$ [0.5]
Answer: (a) 2,704 · 676 · 169 · (b) 3,549
126⭐⭐A rectangular input2 pts · ~3 min
A wide photo is fed as $640 \times 384$ (width × height), strides 8, 16, 32. (a) How many predictions? (b) Why does a program pad a photo only to a multiple of 32 instead of to a square?
Show solution
(a) $80 \times 48 + 40 \times 24 + 20 \times 12 = 3840 + 960 + 240 = 5040$ [1.5]
(b) each side must divide by the largest stride (32) so every grid has whole cells; padding further to a square only adds grey cells to check [0.5]
Answer: (a) 5,040 · (b) multiples of 32 keep the grids whole; a square would waste work on padding
127⭐Numbers per prediction1.5 pts · ~2 min
A detector is fine-tuned for 12 classes and fed $640 \times 640$ images (8,400 predictions). (a) How many numbers does each prediction have? (b) How many numbers in the whole output?
Show solution
(a) 4 for the box + 12 class scores = 16 [0.75]
(b) $8400 \times 16 = 134\,400$ [0.75]
Answer: (a) 16 · (b) 134,400
128⭐⭐Which cell answers?1.5 pts · ~3 min
On the stride-32 grid of a $640 \times 640$ image, an object is centred at $(300, 470)$. (a) Which row and column hold its centre? (b) Where is that cell's centre? (c) A person is only 20 px tall. Which of the three grids is most likely to find them?
Show solution
(a) column $\lfloor 300/32 \rfloor = 9$, row $\lfloor 470/32 \rfloor = 14$ [0.5]
(b) $((9 + \tfrac12) \cdot 32,\ (14 + \tfrac12) \cdot 32) = (304, 464)$ [0.5]
(c) the fine grid, stride 8 — its cells are small enough for a small object [0.5]
Answer: (a) row 14, column 9 · (b) $(304, 464)$ · (c) stride 8
129⭐⭐What fine-tuning changes1.5 pts · ~3 min
You want a detector for 4 kinds of fruit on a market stall, starting from a COCO-trained YOLO. (a) Which part changes, and how many numbers per prediction now? (b) Which parts are reused, and why? (c) What data must you prepare?
Show solution
(a) the head: 80 → 4 classes, so $4 + 4 = 8$ numbers per prediction [0.5]
(b) backbone and neck, as trained on COCO: they already turn photos into useful features — transfer learning (session 4 D) [0.5]
(c) photos of the stall with a box and a class drawn on every fruit, split into train / validation / test [0.5]
Answer: (a) the head, 8 numbers · (b) backbone + neck · (c) labelled boxes on your own photos

C · Segmentation

Slides for this part →
130⭐Mask IoU1.5 pts · ~2 min
A predicted mask has 120 pixels and the true mask 100; 90 pixels are in both. (a) Compute the union. (b) Compute the mask IoU.
Show solution
(a) $120 + 100 - 90 = 130$ [0.75]
(b) $90 / 130 \approx 0.69$ [0.75]
Answer: (a) 130 · (b) about 0.69
131⭐⭐Encoder and decoder sizes2 pts · ~4 min
An encoder halves a $448 \times 448$ image four times. (a) How big is its output? (b) The decoder uses transposed convolutions with $k = 2$, $s = 2$, $p = 0$. Show that each one doubles the size, and list the sizes back to 448. (c) Does $k = 4$, $s = 2$, $p = 1$ also double?
Show solution
(a) $448 / 16 = 28$ [0.5]
(b) $\text{out} = (n - 1)\cdot 2 - 0 + 2 = 2n$ [0.5] · $28 → 56 → 112 → 224 → 448$ [0.5]
(c) $(n - 1)\cdot 2 - 2 + 4 = 2n$ — yes [0.5]
Answer: (a) 28 · (b) 2n each: 56, 112, 224, 448 · (c) yes
132⭐⭐Which prompt gives which mask?1.5 pts · ~3 min
With SAM: (a) you click once on a cyclist's helmet. Which masks might come back? (b) You draw a box around the bicycle only. What do you expect? (c) You want the rider but not the bicycle. What prompt helps?
Show solution
(a) several guesses — the helmet, the head, the whole rider — each with a score; you pick [0.5]
(b) the bicycle: a box says which object and roughly how big [0.5]
(c) a positive click on the rider plus a negative click on the bicycle (or a box around the rider only) [0.5]
Answer: (a) part / larger part / whole · (b) the bicycle · (c) a positive and a negative click
133⭐Box or mask?1 pts · ~2 min
A pole 2 px wide crosses a $100 \times 100$ box from corner to corner. (a) About how many pixels does the pole cover? ($\sqrt{2} \approx 1.41$) (b) What share of the box is the pole?
Show solution
(a) the diagonal is $100\sqrt{2} \approx 141$ px long → $2 \times 141 \approx 282$ px [0.5]
(b) $282 / 10\,000 \approx 3\%$ — a box of a thin, slanted object is almost all background; a mask measures the object itself [0.5]
Answer: (a) about 282 · (b) about 3 %
134⭐⭐⭐Why skip connections?2 pts · ~5 min
An encoder turns a $256 \times 256$ image into a $16 \times 16$ map. (a) How many image pixels does one map cell stand for? (b) A decoder that only enlarges this map draws the mask edge in steps of how many pixels? (c) In a U-Net, the decoder map at $64 \times 64$ has 64 channels and the encoder map of the same size also has 64. What does the skip connection give the decoder, and how many channels after joining them?
Show solution
(a) $256 / 16 = 16$ → a $16 \times 16$ patch, 256 pixels [0.5]
(b) 16 pixels: every cell is all-in or all-out, so edges look blocky [0.5]
(c) the encoder's fine detail (edges) at that size [0.5]; joined side by side: $64 + 64 = 128$ channels [0.5]
Answer: (a) 256 pixels · (b) 16-pixel steps · (c) fine detail; 128 channels

D · Open vocabulary & responsibility

Slides for this part →
135⭐Name a region by cosine1.5 pts · ~3 min
A region's embedding (length 1) is $r = [0.8,\ 0.6]$. Sentence embeddings (length 1): “car” $[1,\ 0]$ · “truck” $[0.6,\ 0.8]$ · “bus” $[0,\ 1]$. (a) Compute the three cosines. (b) Which names pass a cosine threshold of 0.9?
Show solution
(a) car $0.8$ · truck $0.48 + 0.48 = 0.96$ · bus $0.6$ [1]
(b) only “truck” [0.5]
Answer: (a) 0.8, 0.96, 0.6 · (b) truck
136⭐⭐Sigmoid, not softmax2 pts · ~4 min
For one region, OWL-ViT-style scoring uses $\sigma((\cos + b) \cdot s)$ with $b = -0.2$ and $s = 10$. The cosines are “a person” 0.30 and “a cyclist” 0.35. Use $\sigma(1.0) = 0.73$, $\sigma(1.5) = 0.82$, $e^{0.5} \approx 1.65$. (a) Compute both scores. (b) With threshold 0.5, which names does the region get? (c) If a softmax were taken over the two values $1.0$ and $1.5$ instead, what shares would they get — and why is that wrong here?
Show solution
(a) person $\sigma((0.30 - 0.2)\cdot 10) = \sigma(1.0) = 0.73$ · cyclist $\sigma(1.5) = 0.82$ [0.5]
(b) both [0.5]
(c) $1 / (1 + 1.65) \approx 0.38$ and $1.65 / 2.65 \approx 0.62$ [0.5]; a softmax forces the names to compete, but a cyclist is a person — both should be allowed [0.5]
Answer: (a) 0.73 and 0.82 · (b) both · (c) 0.38 / 0.62 — wrong, the names are not exclusive
137⭐A datasheet for your data1.5 pts · ~3 min
Your project uses 800 photos of street food stalls you found online. Write three questions a datasheet (Gebru et al., 2021) would make you answer, and say why each matters.
Show solution
Any three, each with a reason (0.5 each):
- Where did the photos come from, and may you use them? — licence and consent [0.5]
- Who and what is in them? — people who did not agree; which cities and kinds of stall are missing [0.5]
- Who labelled them, and how? — one person's judgement; how disagreements were settled [0.5]
- What should the data not be used for? — e.g. identifying the vendors (or any other, in place of one above)
Answer: e.g. source and permission · who is in it · who labelled it (or what it must not be used for)
138⭐⭐The words decide who is harmed1.5 pts · ~3 min
CLIP's authors classified face photos into a fixed list of labels that included non-human and crime words. Adding the label “child” cut such labels for ages 0–2 from 30.3 % to 2.3 % (Radford et al., 2021). (a) Why can adding one label change the others' results? (b) What does this mean for someone building an open-vocabulary detector?
Show solution
(a) the model must pick from the list it is given; without a fitting label, a child's photo goes to the closest remaining one — even a harmful one [0.75]
(b) the label list is a design decision: include fitting labels, leave out harmful ones, and test the list on the people the system will meet [0.75]
Answer: (a) a forced choice among the given words · (b) choose and test the words with care
139⭐⭐Before you deploy a person counter2 pts · ~4 min
A library wants to count the people entering with a camera and a person detector. (a) Name two questions to answer before installing it. (b) What should the evaluation report, beyond one accuracy number? (c) Suggest a design that needs less personal data.
Show solution
(a) any two of: who agreed and how they are told · what the footage is for and nothing else · who can see it and how long it is kept · the lawful basis under the PDPA [1]
(b) precision and recall by group — e.g. wheelchair users, children, people in groups, at night — plus what it was not tested on [0.5]
(c) count on the device and keep only the number (no images stored), or use a sensor that cannot identify anyone [0.5]
Answer: (a) consent and purpose · (b) results by group and limits · (c) count on the device, store no images

Session 9 · Motion & Video

A · Optical flow

Slides for this part →
140⭐Frames and time1.5 pts · ~3 min
A camera films at 50 frames per second. A ball moves 4 pixels between two frames. (a) How many milliseconds lie between frames? (b) How fast is the ball in pixels per second? (c) At 25 fps, how far does the same ball move between frames?
Show solution
(a) $1000 / 50 = 20$ ms [0.5]
(b) $4 \times 50 = 200$ px/s [0.5]
(c) $200 / 25 = 8$ px per frame — twice as far, so harder for flow to follow [0.5]
Answer: (a) 20 ms · (b) 200 px/s · (c) 8 px
141⭐⭐A wheel with six spokes2 pts · ~4 min
A wheel has 6 identical spokes and turns 3.75 times a second. A camera films it at 24 fps. (a) How far does it turn between frames? (b) Every how many degrees does it look the same? (c) What does the video show — which way, and how fast in turns per second? (d) At what speed would it seem to stand still?
Show solution
(a) $\Delta\theta = 360° \times 3.75 / 24 = 56.25°$ [0.5]
(b) $360° / 6 = 60°$ [0.25]
(c) nearest match $56.25 - 60 = -3.75°$ per frame → it seems to turn backwards, $3.75 \times 24 / 360 = 0.25$ turns per second [0.75]
(d) $60°$ per frame: $60 \times 24 / 360 = 4$ turns per second [0.5]
Answer: (a) 56.25° · (b) 60° · (c) backwards, 0.25 turns/s · (d) 4 turns/s
142⭐One equation per pixel1.5 pts · ~3 min
Use $I_x u + I_y v + I_t = 0$. (a) A pixel has $I_x = 4$, $I_y = 0$, $I_t = -6$. Find what you can of $(u, v)$. (b) Another pixel has $I_x = 0$, $I_y = 5$, $I_t = 10$. Find what you can.
Show solution
(a) $4u - 6 = 0$ → $u = 1.5$ [0.5]; $v$ is not fixed — the edge is vertical, motion along it is invisible [0.25]
(b) $5v + 10 = 0$ → $v = -2$ (2 pixels up) [0.5]; $u$ is not fixed [0.25]
Answer: (a) $u = 1.5$, $v$ unknown · (b) $v = -2$, $u$ unknown
143⭐⭐Normal flow2 pts · ~4 min
A pixel has $I_x = 5$, $I_y = -12$, $I_t = 26$. (a) Find $\lVert \nabla I \rVert$. (b) Find the normal flow: its size and the motion vector it gives. (c) Could the true motion be $(2, 3)$? Check it.
Show solution
(a) $\sqrt{25 + 144} = 13$ [0.5]
(b) $u_\perp = -I_t / \lVert \nabla I \rVert = -26 / 13 = -2$ along $(5, -12)/13$ → $-2 \cdot (5, -12)/13 = (-10/13,\ 24/13) \approx (-0.77,\ 1.85)$ [0.75]
(c) $5 \cdot 2 - 12 \cdot 3 + 26 = 10 - 36 + 26 = 0$ → yes: it satisfies the equation, so it is possible — one pixel cannot tell it apart from the normal flow [0.75]
Answer: (a) 13 · (b) size 2, about (−0.77, 1.85) · (c) yes
Common mistake: taking the normal flow as the motion — it is only the part across the edge.
144⭐⭐Motion field or optical flow?2 pts · ~4 min
For each scene, say whether the motion field (true 3D motion, projected) and the optical flow (moving brightness) agree, and why: (a) a car with a printed logo drives past; (b) a smooth, evenly coloured ball spins in place; (c) the room light is switched on; (d) a barber's pole turns — its stripes seem to climb.
Show solution
(a) agree — texture moves with the surface [0.5]
(b) differ — the surface moves but the picture does not change: motion, no flow [0.5]
(c) differ — brightness changes, nothing moves: flow (or a broken brightness-constancy assumption), no motion [0.5]
(d) differ — the surface turns sideways, the stripes look as if they move up: the aperture problem on long stripes [0.5]
Answer: only (a) agrees

B · Lucas–Kanade

Slides for this part →
145⭐⭐Least squares on three pixels2.5 pts · ~5 min
Three pixels in one window give $(I_x, I_y, I_t)$ = $(1, 0, -2)$, $(0, 3, 3)$ and $(2, 1, -3)$. (a) Write $A^\top A$ and $-A^\top \mathbf{b}$. (b) Solve for $(u, v)$. (c) Check the answer with the third pixel.
Show solution
(a) $A^\top A$ = [1+0+4 0+0+2 / 2 0+9+1] = [5 2 / 2 10] [0.75] · $-A^\top\mathbf{b} = -(1 \cdot (-2) + 2 \cdot (-3),\ 3 \cdot 3 + 1 \cdot (-3)) = (8, -6)$ [0.5]
(b) $\det = 50 - 4 = 46$ → $u = (10 \cdot 8 - 2 \cdot (-6)) / 46 = 92/46 = 2$ · $v = (5 \cdot (-6) - 2 \cdot 8) / 46 = -46/46 = -1$ [1]
(c) $2 \cdot 2 + 1 \cdot (-1) - 3 = 0$ ✓ [0.25]
Answer: (a) [5 2 / 2 10] and (8, −6) · (b) $(u, v) = (2, -1)$
146⭐Solve with a diagonal M1.5 pts · ~3 min
A window has $M$ = [8 0 / 0 4], $\sum I_x I_t = -12$ and $\sum I_y I_t = 6$. (a) Find $(u, v)$. (b) Is this window a corner, an edge or flat?
Show solution
(a) $M (u, v)^\top = (12, -6)$ → $u = 12/8 = 1.5$ [0.5], $v = -6/4 = -1.5$ [0.5]
(b) both eigenvalues (8 and 4) are large → a corner, so the answer can be trusted [0.5]
Answer: (a) (1.5, −1.5) · (b) a corner
147⭐⭐Which window can be solved?2 pts · ~4 min
Three windows: $M_1$ = [6 2 / 2 6], $M_2$ = [4 2 / 2 1], $M_3$ = [0.2 0 / 0 0.1]. For each: $\det M$, the eigenvalues, and whether Lucas–Kanade can find $(u, v)$.
Show solution
$M_1$: $\det = 36 - 4 = 32$ · $\lambda = 6 \pm 2 = 8, 4$ → corner, solvable [0.75]
$M_2$: $\det = 4 - 4 = 0$ · trace 5 → $\lambda = 5, 0$ → edge: no inverse, only the normal flow (aperture problem) [0.75]
$M_3$: $\det = 0.02$ · $\lambda = 0.2, 0.1$ → flat: an answer exists on paper, but noise decides it [0.5]
Answer: only $M_1$ gives a reliable $(u, v)$
148⭐⭐Coarse to fine2 pts · ~4 min
A car moves 40 pixels between frames. Lucas–Kanade only works for motions up to about 3 pixels. (a) How many pyramid levels (each half the size) are needed? (b) At the top level Lucas–Kanade finds 2.5 px. What first guess does that give at the full image?
Show solution
(a) $40 / 2^k \le 3$: $40/8 = 5$ is too big, $40/16 = 2.5$ is fine → $k = 4$ levels [1]
(b) each level down doubles the motion: $2.5 \times 2^4 = 40$ px, then refined at each level [1]
Answer: (a) 4 levels · (b) 40 px
149⭐⭐⭐The same M as Harris2.5 pts · ~5 min
A window has $M$ = [10 6 / 6 10], $\sum I_x I_t = -32$ and $\sum I_y I_t = -16$. (a) Compute the Harris response $R = \det M - 0.04\,(\mathrm{trace}\, M)^2$. Corner or edge? (b) Solve for $(u, v)$. (c) Why does a large $R$ mean Lucas–Kanade can be trusted here?
Show solution
(a) $\det = 100 - 36 = 64$ · trace $= 20$ → $R = 64 - 0.04 \cdot 400 = 48 > 0$ → corner [0.75]
(b) $M (u, v)^\top = (32, 16)$ → $u = (10 \cdot 32 - 6 \cdot 16)/64 = 224/64 = 3.5$ · $v = (10 \cdot 16 - 6 \cdot 32)/64 = -32/64 = -0.5$ [1]
(c) both need the same thing — two large eigenvalues of the same $M$: then $M$ has a stable inverse [0.75]
Answer: (a) 48, a corner · (b) (3.5, −0.5) · (c) same matrix, same condition

C · Tracking

Slides for this part →
150⭐Frame difference1.5 pts · ~3 min
Four pixels change from frame $t-1$ to frame $t$: 40 → 43 · 100 → 160 · 200 → 130 · 90 → 100. (a) With $\tau = 20$, which pixels are “moving”? (b) Why does a car that stops at a red light vanish from the result?
Show solution
(a) differences 3, 60, 70, 10 → only 100 → 160 and 200 → 130 are moving [1]
(b) a still object gives the same values in both frames: difference 0 [0.5]
Answer: (a) the 2nd and 3rd pixel · (b) no change, so nothing is detected
151⭐⭐Normalised cross-correlation2 pts · ~4 min
A template is $t = (2, 4, 6)$. Compute the NCC with the patches (a) $p = (5, 7, 9)$ and (b) $p = (6, 4, 2)$. (c) What does (a) show?
Show solution
(a) $\bar t = 4$, $\bar p = 7$ → deviations $(-2, 0, 2)$ and $(-2, 0, 2)$ → $\dfrac{4 + 0 + 4}{\sqrt{8 \cdot 8}} = 1$ [0.75]
(b) $\bar p = 4$ → deviations $(2, 0, -2)$ → $\dfrac{-4 + 0 - 4}{8} = -1$ [0.75]
(c) a patch made brighter by +3 still matches perfectly — NCC ignores a change of brightness [0.5]
Answer: (a) 1 · (b) −1 (the pattern reversed) · (c) brightness offsets do not matter
152⭐⭐Link two frames by IoU2 pts · ~4 min
Frame $t$: A $(0, 0, 10, 10)$, B $(20, 0, 30, 10)$. Frame $t+1$: P $(2, 0, 12, 10)$, Q $(26, 0, 36, 10)$. (a) Compute IoU(A, P) and IoU(B, Q). (b) Link with threshold 0.3: who keeps an ID, who is lost, who is new? (c) And with threshold 0.2?
Show solution
(a) A–P: $I = 8 \cdot 10 = 80$, $U = 200 - 80 = 120$ → $\approx 0.67$ [0.5] · B–Q: $I = 4 \cdot 10 = 40$, $U = 160$ → $0.25$ [0.5]
(b) A → P keeps its ID · $0.25 < 0.3$: B is lost and Q gets a new ID [0.5]
(c) both pairs link: A → P, B → Q [0.5]
Answer: (a) 0.67 and 0.25 · (b) A→P; B lost, Q new · (c) both linked
153⭐⭐Highest IoU first2 pts · ~4 min
Two tracks A, B and two new boxes P, Q have IoU: A–P 0.7 · B–P 0.5 · B–Q 0.45 · A–Q 0.1. Threshold 0.3. (a) Link them, highest IoU first, each box once. (b) Now A–P is 0.5 and B–P is 0.7 (the rest the same). Link again. (c) What went wrong for A in (b)?
Show solution
(a) A–P 0.7 ✓ · B–P skipped (P taken) · B–Q 0.45 ✓ [0.75]
(b) B–P 0.7 ✓ · A–P skipped · B–Q skipped (B taken) · A–Q $0.1 < 0.3$ ✗ → A is lost, Q gets a new ID [0.75]
(c) B took A's box: two people close together can swap or lose IDs [0.5]
Answer: (a) A→P, B→Q · (b) B→P; A lost, Q new
154⭐⭐Count IDs or crossings?2 pts · ~4 min
A tracker at a shop door reports 52 different IDs in one minute; staff counted 30 people walking in. (a) Give two reasons the IDs over-count. (b) What should the system count instead, and how would you score it? (c) Give one way to keep less personal data.
Show solution
(a) any two: a track breaks when someone is hidden and restarts with a new ID · duplicate boxes on one person · people walking out also get IDs · fast motion or a low frame rate [1]
(b) count crossings of a line (inward only) and compare with a hand count: error $= |\text{count} - 30| / 30$ [0.5]
(c) keep only the totals and drop the tracks · blur faces · process on the device [0.5]
Answer: (a) broken tracks, duplicates · (b) line crossings vs a hand count · (c) store totals, not paths

D · Putting it all together

Slides for this part →
155⭐The budget per frame1.5 pts · ~3 min
A system runs at 20 fps. Its stages take 22 ms (detector), 4 ms (tracker) and 15 ms (counting and drawing). (a) What is the budget per frame? (b) Does it fit, and how much time is left? (c) Would it fit at 30 fps?
Show solution
(a) $1000 / 20 = 50$ ms [0.5]
(b) $22 + 4 + 15 = 41$ ms ≤ 50 → fits, 9 ms spare [0.5]
(c) $1000/30 \approx 33.3$ ms < 41 → no [0.5]
Answer: (a) 50 ms · (b) yes, 9 ms left · (c) no
156⭐⭐Run the slow stage less often2 pts · ~4 min
At 20 fps a pipeline needs: detector 25 ms, tracker 2 ms, segmentation 40 ms. (a) Does it fit when every stage runs on every frame? What frame rate does it reach? (b) Run segmentation on every 2nd frame: average time per frame? (c) Every 4th frame? (d) How long does a frame with segmentation still take?
Show solution
(a) $25 + 2 + 40 = 67$ ms > 50 ✗ → $1000/67 \approx 15$ fps [0.5]
(b) $27 + 40/2 = 47$ ms ✓ on average [0.5]
(c) $27 + 40/4 = 37$ ms ✓ [0.5]
(d) still $67$ ms — those frames come late unless they are buffered [0.5]
Answer: (a) no, about 15 fps · (b) 47 ms · (c) 37 ms · (d) 67 ms
157⭐⭐From pixels to speed2.5 pts · ~5 min
A camera on a bridge watches a road to measure car speeds. (a) Name the session that gives each step: find each car · follow it from frame to frame · map its wheels to metres on the road · check the speeds against a radar. (b) On the road map, a car moves from $(0, 5)$ m to $(0, 17)$ m in 12 frames at 24 fps. What is its speed in m/s and km/h?
Show solution
(a) detector — session 8 · tracking — session 9 · a homography of the road plane — session 7 · a metric on the same data — session 8 [1]
(b) distance $17 - 5 = 12$ m [0.25]; time $12 / 24 = 0.5$ s [0.25]; speed $12 / 0.5 = 24$ m/s [0.5] $= 24 \times 3.6 = 86.4$ km/h [0.5]
Answer: (a) 8 · 9 · 7 · 8 · (b) 24 m/s = 86.4 km/h
158⭐⭐Two solutions, one comparison2 pts · ~4 min
Two solutions count people in the same 10-minute video; a hand count says 50. Solution 1 counts 47 and needs 35 ms per frame; solution 2 counts 41 and needs 8 ms. (a) Compute each count error in %. (b) Which fits at 30 fps? At 25 fps? (c) Which would you choose for a live counter at 25 fps, and why?
Show solution
(a) $|47 - 50|/50 = 6\,\%$ · $|41 - 50|/50 = 18\,\%$ [0.5]
(b) 30 fps → 33.3 ms: only solution 2 [0.5] · 25 fps → 40 ms: both [0.5]
(c) solution 1 — it fits 40 ms and is three times more accurate; same data, same metric, both numbers reported [0.5]
Answer: (a) 6 % and 18 % · (b) 30 fps: solution 2 only; 25 fps: both · (c) solution 1
159⭐Name the risks1.5 pts · ~3 min
A shopping mall wants to track shoppers across its cameras to learn which shops they visit. (a) Name two risks. (b) Name two design choices that reduce them.
Show solution
(a) any two: paths of identifiable people are personal data (PDPA) · tracks joined across cameras show a person's whole visit · people did not agree · the footage could be used for something else [0.75]
(b) any two: keep counts per shop, not paths · delete tracks after counting · blur faces · tell visitors and state the purpose · limit who can see the data [0.75]
Answer: (a) e.g. personal paths, no consent · (b) e.g. totals only, short retention
